analysis.one_liner: Caps payday loan interest at 36% and tightly licenses payday lenders nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill to cap payday loan rates never left committee: it died in the House Financial Services Committee after getting just one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make payday lending illegal in any state that doesn't license and strictly regulate payday lenders. It caps interest at 36% a year (or the state's own cap, if lower), limits loans to $300, bans rolling a loan over into a new one, bans using criminal charges to collect, and bans forced arbitration clauses. Banks would be barred from making payday loans above the cap or from financing payday lenders who break the rules. It died without ever getting a committee vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income borrowers who use payday loans: they would keep access to small, short-term credit but at far lower rates, shorter terms limited to $300, no debt-roll-over traps, no criminal threats for a bounced check, and no mandatory arbitration clauses. States that want to shut payday lending down or cap rates would gain the power to do so, and the Federal Reserve would decide which state laws qualify.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual interest rate on payday loans at the lesser of 36% or the state's maximum for comparable small loans, versus the triple-digit annual rates typical of the industry [S3].
Limits each loan to $300 principal, requires a minimum term of two weeks per $50 borrowed, caps administrative fees at $5, and caps bounced-check fees at $15 [S3].
Bans rolling over or refinancing a payday loan, bans issuing a new loan within 30 days, and bans accepting repayment funded by another payday loan — targeting the repeat-borrowing cycle [S3].

Prohibits criminal actions or threats of criminal prosecution for failing to repay, requires written and posted disclosures of borrower rights, and bans mandatory binding arbitration clauses in loan documents [S3].

Requires states to license payday lenders with background checks, $50,000 surety bonds per location, public hearings, complaint handling, and civil and criminal penalties, and gives borrowers a private right to sue for damages and attorney's fees [S3].
Bars banks from making payday loans above the rate cap and from financing payday lenders who are not in full compliance with federal and state law [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Payday lenders, whose standard business model of triple-digit annual rates and repeat borrowing would be squeezed to near unprofitability; and banks, including those chartering payday lenders through bank-partnership arrangements, which could no longer make or finance loans above the cap. Borrowers in states that choose not to license payday lending would lose access to these loans entirely.

drawbacks.text: In states that decline to meet the federal licensing requirements, payday loans would become outright illegal, cutting off a source of fast cash for borrowers who may have no alternative when facing an emergency expense [S3].

A 36% rate cap plus a $5 fee cap on loans averaging two weeks would likely make the product unprofitable at traditional storefront scale, so even borrowers who want the credit could lose it — the classic tradeoff of rate caps [S3].

Critics of rate caps generally argue borrowers pushed out of payday loans turn to costlier options like overdrafts, pawn shops, or unlicensed lenders; the bill contains no substitute source of small-dollar emergency credit [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers who keep access, the bill is a large gain: a 36% cap versus rates that commonly run several hundred percent a year, plus an end to rollover debt spirals and criminal-threat collection. The real cost falls on borrowers in states that choose not to license payday lending, who would have no legal payday option at all, and the bill offers no alternative for their emergency credit needs. The design trades some access for much lower cost and far stronger legal protections.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and then to its subcommittee on financial institutions, and no vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Rush introduced the Payday Borrower Protection Act of 2005 on April 14, 2005 [S1][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, and on May 19, 2005 to its Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].
The bill attracted only one cosponsor over its entire two-year life [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday lenders and the banks financing them kept operating under the pre-existing rules, with no rate cap, no licensing regime, and no ban on rollovers or arbitration clauses.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Payday lenders and their bank financiers

for.name: Rep. Bobby Rush
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor [S1][S5].

for.name: 1 House Democrat
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsor it ever received [S4].

against.name: House Financial Services Committee

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; it died in the committee and its subcommittee [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill never progressed far enough to reveal a party split; it had one Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor and no recorded votes or stated opposition.

industries.note: A 36% rate cap, $5 fee cap, $300 loan limit, and ban on rollovers would eliminate the core of the storefront payday model, which depends on triple-digit annual rates and repeat borrowing. Their gain is borrowers' cost.

Banks would be barred from making payday loans above 36% and from financing payday lenders out of compliance with state and federal law, ending the bank-partnership route around state rate caps. Banks making compliant loans under 36% could continue.
The bill bans mandatory binding arbitration clauses in payday loan contracts, keeping borrower disputes in court where damages and attorney's fees are available [S3].
